Nokoni

Nokoni is a historical Comanche band/division name with its own directory route. The Texas report connects the name with a wider history of local bands and divisions and describes a historical range extending beyond today’s Texas boundary. Anderson’s account of the 1868–1869 winter campaign provides a specifically named episode involving Horseback’s Nokoni camp. It should be read as an outside military-history interpretation, alongside further community histories and original records.

Names & relationshipsThe December 2021 report identifies this name within historical Comanche band/division organization. This is a historical name-only access route linked to the broader Comanche collection, not a newly established separate people, present-day government, citizenship category or exclusive descendant group. The report describes band formation and political organization as fluid. Printed spellings in the inspected December 2021 synthesis, attributed there to CLCPC 2010. They are not independently verified community-preferred present orthography; no translations or pronunciation claims are adopted.

These photographs have individual, documented connections to this entry. Their captions and source records define the people, place, object, and period shown; no one photograph represents every community within a broader label.

Portrait in the NARA record naming Horseback, a Nakoney chief, and his bodyguard
William S. Soule; National Archives, NAID 533053, local identifier 165-AI-12 / Wikimedia Commons. Public domain in the United States. Archival title names Horseback, a Nakoney chief, and his bodyguard; the retrieved frame shows one sitter.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain in the United States — NARA/Commons federal-work media notice

The exact NARA-derived Commons item title names Fer-ha-yer-quoip/Old Horseback as a Nakoney chief and mentions his bodyguard; the actual complete 2090-by-3000 downloaded JPEG contains ONE seated man. This caption/frame mismatch remains explicit. The photograph is presented as a portrait within that specifically identified Nokoni-related archival record, not as a newly verified identification of the visible individual. Do not name the seated person more confidently, infer an unseen second person or crop to suggest an identification. Hugh Allen Anderson's TSHA account explicitly identifies Horseback's Nokoni band; that supports the named record's band relevance, not a visual identification. Commons credits Soule, preserves the War Department record creator and NAID 533053/local identifier 165-AI-12, and includes a specific federal-work public-domain notice. Its 1881–1885 series-compilation date does not resolve Soule's earlier exposure date. The entire available JPEG frame and edge imperfections were visually inspected; no retouching, pixel crop, generated content or restoration was performed. Root may make a disclosed proportional 1800px derivative; retain full frame on the opened page and disclose CSS display crops. Image review adds no substantive reading-work count. 01

Read the name within a fluid band structure

The consulted report places Nokoni among named historical Comanche divisions and notes relationships with smaller local groups. It describes bands forming and separating through family and political relationships. These changing arrangements should not be converted into a fixed modern nation list or an exclusive genealogy.

Read the sources [1] Texas Department of Transportation

02

Winter provisions and community survival

Anderson identifies the camp attacked at Soldier Spring as Horseback’s Nokoni village. His account describes the destruction of stored food needed for winter and later movement toward federal posts. This focused episode opens questions about families, survival and diplomacy; original military reports and community accounts remain separate research tasks.

Read the sources [2] Texas State Historical Association / Handbook of Texas Online; Hugh Allen Anderson

TxDOT Tribal Histories: Comanche Nation Research Report — selected pages ↗

Texas Department of Transportation. 2021. TxDOT Tribal Histories: Comanche Nation Research Report. December. Selected pages.

Publication: 2021-12

A chronological Texas synthesis prepared with the Nation’s historic-preservation office. Selected text supports a regional starting guide; its sources, dates and interpretations still need comparison.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Downloaded actual72-page PDF and read selected text: printed/PDFpp3,6–10,35–36,50–54. Map images and cited originals were not inspected; no sensitive-site locations or ceremonial instructions are reproduced.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public text inspected

Access note: Browser fetch timed out; official file downloaded successfully and selected pages extracted with pypdf. Review is textual, not visual inspection of illustrations. Internal chronology includes Texas annexation as1846 onp36 and a March1882 visit after1891 onp54; these dates are not adopted. Evaluative claims about individual leaders and reported historical counts remain outside this synthesis. Consultation does not make every statement independently verified.

Canadian River Expedition — selected Nokoni camp and winter-campaign account ↗

An outside military-history account that specifically identifies Horseback’s Nokoni camp at Soldier Spring and describes the destruction of winter provisions and subsequent movement. Its military framing, labels and broad opening chronology require comparison with Indigenous histories; casualty figures and current legal conclusions are not adopted.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual complete main body and bibliography read, web lines6–28. Synthesis limited to the Soldier Spring camp, winter provisions and subsequent Nokoni movement, especially16–21. Opening Washita chronology, casualty totals, military justifications, underlying reports and cited books are not adopted or independently verified.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access note: Public HTML main body inspected. Bibliography points to further works; those underlying publications and original records were not read here.

https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/canadian-river-expedition
